clm() writes these slopes as shifts of the thresholds, so the effect of security on a higher answer is the number shown with its sign changed: 0.20, 0.32, 0.45 at the three splits. The likelihood-ratio test is the same as the security row of nominal_test(), and the AIC is a little worse: two more parameters that do not pay for themselves. We keep the simple model. If several predictors failed, the alternatives are a model with every slope free (nominal = ~ ., the generalized ordered logit) or the multinomial model.

Four more things to keep in mind

Code 
# answers given as categories instead of numbers: one coefficient per answer
fit_steps <- update(fit, . ~ . - autonomy - respect - security - stress +
                      factor(autonomy) + factor(respect) + factor(security) + factor(stress))
steps_test <- anova(fit, fit_steps)
stress_steps <- coef(fit_steps)[paste0("factor(stress)", 2:5)]   # hardly ever ... always, against never
# the people who answered on the web against those interviewed in person or by phone
very_by_mode <- prop.table(table(d$web, d$satisfaction), 1)[, "Very satisfied"]
fit_mode <- update(fit, . ~ . + web)
round(cbind(without_mode = coef(fit), with_mode = coef(fit_mode)[names(coef(fit))]), 2)
                 without_mode with_mode
autonomy                 0.39      0.39
respect                  0.73      0.73
security                 0.38      0.37
stress                  -0.38     -0.37
homeSome days            0.16      0.17
homeMainly              -0.08     -0.06
self_employedYes         0.45      0.44
age10                    0.15      0.15
  • Equal steps. The four scored questions count each step up the scale the same. Treating the answers as categories instead, with a coefficient for each answer, fits somewhat better, \(\chi^2\)(9) = 21.73, p = .010: the steps are not all equal. For stress, for example, the coefficients of “hardly ever”, “sometimes”, “often” and “always” against “never” are -0.64, -0.83, -1.41, -1.59, not evenly spaced. The scored model is easier to read and tells the same story.
  • Web or interview. In 2022 most people answered the GSS on the web. 41% of them said “very satisfied”, against 49% of those interviewed in person or by phone, as people often give more positive answers when an interviewer is listening. Adding the mode to the model leaves the other coefficients almost unchanged (above).
  • The sample, not the population. These are unweighted estimates for the people in the survey. To describe all US workers, use the GSS weights (wtssps) and the design of the survey, for example with svyolr() in the package survey (Lumley, 2010).
  • Association, not cause. People who like their work may also see their workplace in a better light, and judge it more respectful and more secure. One survey at one point in time cannot tell which comes first.

8. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the outcome and its order, the predictors and how they were scored, the model test, the check of the proportional odds assumption and the odds ratios with their uncertainty. The numbers come from the R objects, so the text below always matches the results:

Code 
n_model <- nrow(d)
lr      <- model_test$"LR stat."[2]
lr_df   <- model_test$"   Df"[2]
lr_p    <- model_test$"Pr(Chi)"[2]
ci_text <- function(t) paste0("95% CI [", f2(ci[t, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[t, 2]), "]")

Method (data analysis):

We analysed the 2,167 employed respondents to the 2022 General Social Survey (Davern et al., 2024) who answered the job satisfaction question and the Quality of Working Life questions used here. Job satisfaction (very dissatisfied, a little dissatisfied, moderately satisfied, very satisfied) was analysed with an ordinal logistic regression (proportional odds model). The predictors were autonomy, respect at work and job security (each scored 1–4) and work stress (scored 1–5), with higher scores meaning more; how often the respondent worked from home (never, some days, mainly); self-employment; and age. The proportional odds assumption was checked with likelihood-ratio tests of nominal effects. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the MASS (Venables & Ripley, 2002) and ordinal (Christensen, 2026) packages.

Results:

The predictors improved the fit over a thresholds-only model, χ²(8) = 566.95, p < .001, McFadden’s R² = .12, and no predictor departed from the proportional odds assumption (smallest p = .166). Holding the other predictors constant, respondents who felt more respected at work were more satisfied with their job, OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.80, 2.39], as were those with more autonomy, OR = 1.48, 95% CI [1.32, 1.67], and better job security, OR = 1.47, 95% CI [1.31, 1.64]. More frequent stress went with lower satisfaction, OR = 0.69, 95% CI [0.62, 0.75]. Self-employed and older respondents were more satisfied (Table 1). How often respondents worked from home was not related to job satisfaction once the other predictors were held constant, χ²(2) = 3.66, p = .161.

Table 1

Odds Ratios From an Ordinal Logistic Regression of Job Satisfaction, General Social Survey 2022

Predictor Odds ratio 95% CI p
Autonomy (per step) 1.48 [1.32, 1.67] < .001
Respect (per step) 2.07 [1.80, 2.39] < .001
Job security (per step) 1.47 [1.31, 1.64] < .001
Stress (per step) 0.69 [0.62, 0.75] < .001
Works from home some days (vs never) 1.17 [0.96, 1.43] .130
Works mainly from home (vs never) 0.93 [0.73, 1.17] .527
Self-employed (vs employee) 1.57 [1.19, 2.08] .001
Age (per 10 years) 1.16 [1.09, 1.24] < .001

Note. N = 2,167. Odds ratios above 1 mean higher job satisfaction. Autonomy, respect and job security were scored 1–4 and stress 1–5, higher scores meaning more; age is in decades. Confidence intervals are profile-likelihood intervals.

Points to remember:

  • Say which way the outcome runs, and whether an odds ratio above 1 means a higher or a lower answer: programs differ.
  • Report odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and say that they hold the other predictors constant.
  • Give the model test (\(\chi^2\) with its degrees of freedom) and a pseudo-\(R^2\), and say which one.
  • Report the check of the proportional odds assumption, and what you did if it failed.
  • Predicted probabilities for typical people are easier to understand than odds ratios; show them where they help.
  • Cite R and the packages; citation("MASS") and citation("ordinal") give the references.

9. Summary

When The outcome is a category with three or more values in a natural order
Why not linear regression It assumes equal steps between the answers and predicts values nobody can give
Why not multinomial logistic regression It ignores the order and needs a set of coefficients for every answer
How (R) MASS::polr(y ~ x, data, Hess = TRUE), with y an ordered factor; or ordinal::clm()
Output Thresholds (one per split) and one slope per predictor; exp() of a slope is a cumulative odds ratio
Easiest to read Predicted probabilities: predict(fit, newdata, type = "probs")
Tests Likelihood-ratio tests with anova() and drop1(); McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\)
Assumptions Independent observations; proportional odds (the same slopes at every split)
If proportional odds fails A partial proportional odds model, clm(..., nominal = ~ x); or a multinomial model

References

Agresti, A. (2010). Analysis of ordinal categorical data (2nd ed.). Wiley.

Brant, R. (1990). Assessing proportionality in the proportional odds model for ordinal logistic regression. Biometrics, 46(4), 1171–1178. https://doi.org/10.2307/2532457

Christensen, R. H. B. (2026). ordinal: Regression models for ordinal data (R package version 2026.7-26). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ordinal

Davern, M., Bautista, R., Freese, J., Herd, P., & Morgan, S. L. (2024). General Social Survey 1972–2022 (Release 4) [Data set]. NORC at the University of Chicago. https://gss.norc.org/

Lumley, T. (2010). Complex surveys: A guide to analysis using R. Wiley.

McCullagh, P. (1980). Regression models for ordinal data. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 42(2), 109–142.

Peterson, B., & Harrell, F. E., Jr. (1990). Partial proportional odds models for ordinal response variables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series C (Applied Statistics), 39(2), 205–217.

Venables, W. N., & Ripley, B. D. (2002). Modern applied statistics with S (4th ed.). Springer.

Wickham, H., Miller, E., & Smith, D. (2025). haven: Import and export ‘SPSS’, ‘Stata’ and ‘SAS’ files (R package version 2.5.5). https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.haven

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
item.description: Multinomial logistic regression in R with nnet::multinom(), on real OPM data: how about 330,000 US federal employees left their jobs in fiscal year 2025 (quit, retired, early retirement, deferred resignation, laid off, terminated), with relative risk ratios, predicted probabilities, the IIA assumption and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Multinomial logistic regression in R with nnet::multinom(), on real OPM data: how about 330,000 US federal employees left their jobs in fiscal year 2025 (quit, retired, early retirement, deferred resignation, laid off, terminated), with relative risk ratios, predicted probabilities, the IIA assumption and APA reporting.

The question: six ways to leave

In 2025 the US federal government lost staff in several ways at once. In January, most federal employees were offered a deferred resignation: stop working, stay on the payroll until 30 September 2025, then resign. Agencies offered early retirement, carried out reductions in force (layoffs) and dismissed staff. And people kept quitting and retiring, as they do every year.

So everyone who left federal service in 2025 left in one of six ways. This page asks: among the people who left, what made one way of leaving more likely than another? Did the young quit and the old retire? Who took the deferred resignation? Who was laid off?

The outcome is a category with six values and no natural order: quitting is not “more” or “less” than being laid off. The type of outcome decides the type of regression:

Outcome Regression Example
Two categories logistic hired or not
Ordered categories ordinal logistic a performance rating from 1 to 5
Unordered categories multinomial logistic how someone left: quit, retired, laid off…

A multinomial logistic regression picks one category as the reference and fits a logistic regression of each of the other categories against it, all at the same time. The data are real: the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) publishes a record for every federal employee who leaves.

Code 
library(nnet)         # multinom(): multinomial logistic regression (comes with R)
library(nanoparquet)  # read_parquet(): reads the Parquet files that OPM publishes
library(ggplot2)
# one colour per way of leaving, the same in every chart
exits   <- c("Quit", "Retired", "Early retirement", "Deferred resignation", "Laid off", "Terminated")
colours <- setNames(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300"), exits)
ink     <- setNames(c("white", "white", "white", "#0b0b0b", "white", "white"), exits)  # labels on the bars
# number formats for the text
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
rr   <- function(x) ifelse(x >= 100, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","),
                           formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))                   # relative risk ratios

1. The data

OPM’s Federal Workforce Data has a file for every month with one row per separation: a civilian employee leaving federal service. Each row says how the person left, their age group, years of service, agency, occupation, type of appointment and more. The files are free, need no login, and come through an API as Parquet files of one to four MB.

A monthly file holds the separations processed in that month, and some of them took effect months earlier: separations of September 2025 were still arriving in 2026. So we download every file from October 2023 to the latest one, and sort the separations by the date they took effect.

Code 
options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # allow slow downloads
# the list of monthly files, with the current version of each
files <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations?current=true")
files <- files[as.integer(files$year) * 100 + as.integer(files$month) >= 202310, ]
latest <- max(as.Date(paste(files$year, files$month, "01", sep = "-")))
# the columns we need, out of the 69 in each file
columns <- c("personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm", "separation_category", "drp_indicator",
             "age_bracket", "length_of_service_years", "supervisory_status",
             "appointment_type", "stem_occupation")
# one month: download the file and read the columns; try again if OPM asks us to slow down
read_month <- function(year, month, version) {
  url  <- sprintf("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations/%s/%s/%s/download", year, month, version)
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
  for (attempt in 1:3) {
    ok <- tryCatch(download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE) == 0, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (ok) break
    Sys.sleep(10 * attempt)
  }
  if (!ok) stop("Could not download ", url)
  as.data.frame(read_parquet(path, col_select = columns))
}
raw <- do.call(rbind, Map(read_month, files$year, files$month, files$version))
nrow(raw)
[1] 808769

That is 36 monthly files, up to September 2026. The US federal fiscal year runs from October to September: fiscal year 2025 (FY2025) is October 2024 to September 2025. We keep FY2024, a year before the changes, and FY2025:

Code 
ym <- as.integer(raw$personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm)   # e.g. 202509 = September 2025
raw$month       <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", ym %/% 100, ym %% 100))
raw$fiscal_year <- ym %/% 100 + (ym %% 100 >= 10)              # October 2024 to September 2025 = 2025
d <- subset(raw, fiscal_year %in% 2024:2025)
table(d$separation_category, d$fiscal_year)
                                    
                                       2024   2025
  OTHER SEPARATION                    16296  17123
  QUIT                                81772 159332
  REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)               33  10417
  RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT                206  20916
  RETIREMENT - OTHER                   3644   5249
  RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY              55567 102490
  TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)    32141  37372
  TRANSFER OUT - INDIVIDUAL TRANSFER  33003  16288
  TRANSFER OUT - MASS TRANSFER          169     84

OPM records how each separation was processed. A separate column, drp_indicator, says whether it came under the deferred resignation programme (Y):

Code 
with(subset(d, fiscal_year == 2025), table(separation_category, drp_indicator))
                                    drp_indicator
separation_category                      N     Y
  OTHER SEPARATION                   17069    54
  QUIT                               94970 64362
  REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)           10416     1
  RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT              8525 12391
  RETIREMENT - OTHER                  5173    76
  RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY             69798 32692
  TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)   36907   465
  TRANSFER OUT - INDIVIDUAL TRANSFER 16259    29
  TRANSFER OUT - MASS TRANSFER          83     1

On paper, most people who took the deferred resignation quit or retired. But they took a different route from people who quit or retired in the ordinary way, so we give them a category of their own. The six ways of leaving:

Way of leaving OPM category What it means
Quit QUIT Resigned
Retired RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY, RETIREMENT - OTHER Retired on a pension
Early retirement RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT Took the agency’s offer of an early pension: age 50 with 20 years of service, or any age with 25 years
Deferred resignation any of the above with drp_indicator = Y Accepted the 2025 offer; most left on 30 September 2025
Laid off REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF) The position was abolished
Terminated TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER) A temporary appointment ended, or the agency ended the employment, for example during the probationary period

We leave out transfers to another agency (those people are still federal employees) and “other separation”, which includes deaths.

Code 
exit <- c("QUIT"                             = "Quit",
          "RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY"           = "Retired",
          "RETIREMENT - OTHER"               = "Retired",
          "RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT"           = "Early retirement",
          "REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)"         = "Laid off",
          "TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)" = "Terminated")[d$separation_category]
exit[!is.na(exit) & d$drp_indicator %in% "Y"] <- "Deferred resignation"
d$exit <- factor(exit, levels = exits)
d <- subset(d, !is.na(exit))     # drops the transfers and the other separations

The predictors are five characteristics of each person. Years of service are cut where the rules change: the first year is usually a probationary period, early retirement needs 20 or 25 years, and a full pension needs, for example, 30 years from age 55 to 57 or 20 years at age 60.

Code 
age <- ifelse(d$age_bracket %in% c("LESS THAN 20", "20-24"), "Under 25",
       ifelse(d$age_bracket == "65 OR MORE", "65+", d$age_bracket))
d$age <- factor(age, levels = c("Under 25", "25-29", "30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49",
                                "50-54", "55-59", "60-64", "65+"))
years <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d$length_of_service_years))
years[years > 60] <- NA          # a few impossible values (up to 1,800 years of service)
d$service <- cut(years, c(-Inf, 1, 5, 10, 20, 25, 30, Inf), right = FALSE,
                 labels = c("Under 1", "1-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-24", "25-29", "30+"))
# supervisors and managers; team leaders count as non-supervisors
supervisors  <- c("SUPERVISOR OR MANAGER", "SUPERVISOR (CSRA)", "MANAGEMENT OFFICIAL (CSRA)")
d$supervisor <- factor(ifelse(d$supervisory_status == "INVALID", NA,
                              ifelse(d$supervisory_status %in% supervisors, "Yes", "No")),
                       levels = c("No", "Yes"))
# a permanent or a temporary (nonpermanent) appointment
d$permanent <- factor(ifelse(d$appointment_type == "INVALID", NA,
                             ifelse(grepl("NONPERMANENT", d$appointment_type), "No", "Yes")),
                      levels = c("Yes", "No"))
# STEM, health or other occupations; "UNSPECIFIED" becomes NA
d$occupation <- factor(c("ALL OTHER OCCUPATIONS" = "Other", "STEM OCCUPATIONS" = "STEM",
                         "HEALTH OCCUPATIONS" = "Health")[d$stem_occupation],
                       levels = c("Other", "STEM", "Health"))
vars <- c("exit", "age", "service", "supervisor", "permanent", "occupation")
d    <- d[complete.cases(d[vars]), ]
fy25 <- subset(d, fiscal_year == 2025)
table(d$fiscal_year)

  2024   2025 
172225 329911

Each row is a separation, not a person: someone who left two temporary jobs in a year is in the data twice. We still call them people, for short.

2. Look at the data

Code 
monthly <- as.data.frame(table(month = d$month, exit = d$exit), responseName = "people")
monthly$month <- as.Date(as.character(monthly$month))
ggplot(monthly, aes(month, people, fill = exit)) +
  geom_col(width = 25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2024-09-16"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ exit, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(title = "Federal employees leaving each month, by how they left",
       subtitle = "October 2023 to September 2025; each panel has its own scale.\nDashed line: the start of fiscal year 2025.",
       x = NULL, y = "people") +
  theme_bw()
Code 
drp_september <- sum(fy25$exit == "Deferred resignation" & fy25$month == as.Date("2025-09-01"))
# terminations of people with under five years of service, February to May
new_terminated <- with(subset(d, exit == "Terminated" & service %in% c("Under 1", "1-4") &
                                 format(month, "%m") %in% c("02", "03", "04", "05")),
                       table(fiscal_year))
new_terminated
fiscal_year
 2024  2025 
 4541 10163

In FY2024, left of the dashed line, people quit, retired or came to the end of a temporary job. Retirements peak every December, and terminations every autumn, when seasonal jobs end. FY2025 is different:

  • Deferred resignations: 106,795 took effect in September 2025 alone, when the paid leave ended.
  • Early retirements and layoffs, almost absent in FY2024, start in spring 2025.
  • Terminations of people with under five years of service rose from 4,541 in February to May 2024 to 10,163 in the same months of 2025, when agencies dismissed many employees who were still in their probationary period.
Code 
counts <- table(d$exit, d$fiscal_year)
data.frame(exit   = exits,
           FY2024 = num(as.vector(counts[, "2024"])),
           FY2025 = num(as.vector(counts[, "2025"])),
           FY2025_share = pct(as.vector(prop.table(counts[, "2025"])), 1))
                  exit FY2024  FY2025 FY2025_share
1                 Quit 81,304  93,341        28.3%
2              Retired 58,643  70,988        21.5%
3     Early retirement    206   8,523         2.6%
4 Deferred resignation      0 109,938        33.3%
5             Laid off     31  10,374         3.1%
6           Terminated 32,041  36,747        11.1%
Code 
top_exit <- names(which.max(counts[, "2025"]))

In FY2025, 329,911 people left in these six ways, 1.9 times as many as in FY2024, and the most common way to leave was the deferred resignation. From here on we use FY2025. Who left which way?

Code 
# stacked bars of shares (each bar adds up to 100%), with the larger shares labelled
stacked <- function(m, y_label, x_label) {
  ggplot(m, aes(share, group, fill = exit)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.8, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(share >= 0.07, pct(share), ""), colour = exit),
              position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colours) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = ink, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = y_label, fill = NULL) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(5.5, 18, 5.5, 5.5)) +  # room for "100%"
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
# how the people in each group left, in FY2025
mix <- function(group, label) {
  m <- as.data.frame(prop.table(table(group = fy25[[group]], exit = fy25$exit), 1), responseName = "share")
  stacked(m, label, "share of the people in the group who left in FY2025")
}
mix("age", "age")
Code 
mix("service", "years of service")
Code 
share      <- function(group) prop.table(table(fy25[[group]], fy25$exit), 1)
by_age     <- share("age")
by_service <- share("service")
by_job     <- share("occupation")
middle     <- c("30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49", "50-54", "55-59", "60-64")
  • Quitting is the usual way out up to age 45; from 50 on, people retire.
  • Early retirement happens at 50 to 59 and with 20 to 29 years of service: the eligibility rules.
  • The deferred resignation is the odd one: between 32% and 38% of the people in every age group from 30 to 64 took it, and a similar share at every length of service from one year up. Ordinary quitting and retiring each belong to one end of a career; the deferred resignation drew from all of it.
  • Layoffs hit the middle of careers: 8.7% of the people aged 45 to 49 who left, 7.6% of those with 10 to 19 years of service.
  • Terminations belong to the young and the new: 36% of the people under 25 and 35% of those with less than a year of service.
  • Occupations differ too: only 4.5% of the people in health occupations took the deferred resignation, against 45% in STEM and 34% in other occupations. Agencies could exclude positions from the offer.

Age and years of service go together, so these charts cannot tell whether age or service drives an exit. The model can: it estimates each effect holding the others constant.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a reference category

Choose one way of leaving as the yardstick. We use Quit, an ordinary resignation: every other way of leaving is compared with quitting. Any category could be the reference; the predicted probabilities are the same, only the comparisons in the output change. In R the reference is the first level of the factor (levels(fy25$exit)[1] is Quit), and relevel() changes it.

Step 2: one equation for every other category

For person \(i\) and each way of leaving \(k\) other than quitting:

\[\eta_{ik} = \ln\frac{P(\text{exit}_i = k)}{P(\text{exit}_i = \text{Quit})} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k}x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_{pk}x_{pi}\]

That is five equations, each with its own intercept and its own slopes. The left side is the log of the relative risk: how much more likely leaving by \(k\) is than quitting. Each equation looks like a logistic regression; the difference is that the five are estimated together, so that every person’s six probabilities add up to 1.

Step 3: from the equations to probabilities

\[P(\text{exit}_i = \text{Quit}) = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{j} e^{\eta_{ij}}} \qquad P(\text{exit}_i = k) = \frac{e^{\eta_{ik}}}{1 + \sum_{j} e^{\eta_{ij}}}\]

The sums run over the five categories other than Quit. Each probability is between 0 and 1, and the six add up to 1. This is the softmax function, the same formula that neural networks use to classify.

Step 4: what a coefficient means

\(e^{\beta}\) is the relative risk ratio (RRR): the number by which the ratio \(P(k)/P(\text{Quit})\) is multiplied when the predictor moves from its reference level to this level, with the other predictors held constant. An RRR of 2 means twice as likely to leave by \(k\) rather than by quitting. Some books and programs call it an odds ratio; either way it compares two categories with each other, not one category with all the others.

Step 5: how R finds the β’s

By maximum likelihood: R looks for the \(\beta\)’s that make the exits that people actually took as probable as possible,

\[\ln L = \sum_i \ln P(\text{exit}_i = \text{the exit that person } i \text{ took})\]

multinom() maximises it. It fits the model as a neural network without a hidden layer, which is why it lives in the package nnet.

Step 6: count the parameters

A predictor with \(c\) categories gets \(c - 1\) coefficients: age has 10 groups (9 coefficients), service 7 (6), supervisor and appointment 2 each (1 each) and occupation 3 (2). That is 19 slopes plus an intercept, 20 per equation, and 5 equations make 100 parameters. Multinomial models grow fast: every category needs enough people for a whole set of coefficients of its own.

4. Fitting the model

Every predictor is a category, so the 329,911 people fall into a limited number of combinations of age group, service, supervisor, appointment, occupation and exit. Fitting the model to the count of people in each combination gives the same estimates as fitting the people one by one: 300 people with the same values add the same term to the log-likelihood 300 times, which is what weights = Freq does. It takes a second instead of minutes.

Code 
g <- as.data.frame(table(fy25[vars]))   # one row per combination; Freq = the number of people
g <- subset(g, Freq > 0)
nrow(g)
[1] 2416
Code 
fit <- multinom(exit ~ age + service + supervisor + permanent + occupation,
                data = g, weights = Freq, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE, Hess = TRUE)
summary(fit)
Call:

    occupation, data = g, weights = Freq, Hess = TRUE, maxit = 1000, 
    trace = FALSE)
